questions.q: Why does the image $\ell(\mathcal{O}_K^\times)$ of the logarithmic embedding lie inside the trace-zero hyperplane $H=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{r_1+r_2}:\sum_i x_i=0\}$?
choices: Because units always have integer trace.
Because the product formula $\prod_v|u|_v=1$ for units, applied across archimedean places, gives $\sum_i\log|\sigma_i(u)|+2\sum_j\log|\tau_j(u)|=0$.
Because $\mathcal{O}_K^\times$ is finitely generated.
Because the embedding is by definition projection onto $H$.
questions.explain: Units satisfy $|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(u)|=1$. Taking logarithms, $\sum_i\log|\sigma_i(u)|+\sum_j\log|\tau_j(u)|^2=\log|N(u)|=0$. The complex coordinates carry weight $2$ exactly because each complex place $\tau_j$ contributes $|\tau_j(u)|^2$ to the absolute norm — so the log-vector lands in the codimension-1 hyperplane $\sum x_i=0$.

questions.q: What is the kernel of the logarithmic embedding $\ell\colon\mathcal{O}_K^\times\to\mathbb{R}^{r_1+r_2}$?
choices: The trivial group $\{1\}$.
The group $\mu_K$ of roots of unity in $K$.
The full unit group $\mathcal{O}_K^\times$.
questions.explain: $\ell(u)=0$ means $|\sigma_i(u)|=1$ for every archimedean place. Such an algebraic integer with all conjugates on the unit circle is a root of unity by Kronecker's theorem. Conversely every root of unity has all conjugates of absolute value $1$, so $\ker\ell=\mu_K$, which is finite (it's a finite subgroup of $K^\times$, hence cyclic).

questions.q: How many archimedean places does $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_5)$ have? (One real place + one complex place each count as a single archimedean place; signature $(r_1,r_2)$ means $r_1+r_2$ archimedean places.)
questions.explain: $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_5)$ has degree $\varphi(5)=4$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, with signature $(0,2)$: no real embeddings (since $\zeta_5\notin\mathbb{R}$) and two pairs of complex-conjugate embeddings. So $r_1+r_2=0+2=2$ archimedean places, and the trace-zero hyperplane $H\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ is $1$-dimensional, giving unit rank $1$.

questions.q: What is the unit rank of $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2})$?
questions.explain: The minimal polynomial $x^3-2$ has one real root $\sqrt[3]{2}$ and one complex-conjugate pair $\zeta_3\sqrt[3]{2},\zeta_3^2\sqrt[3]{2}$, so signature $(r_1,r_2)=(1,1)$. Dirichlet's rank is $r_1+r_2-1=1+1-1=1$, so $\mathcal{O}_K^\times\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\times\mathbb{Z}$ — generated by $-1$ and one fundamental unit (a famous one is $\varepsilon=\sqrt[3]{2}-1$ with $\log|\varepsilon|<0$, $\varepsilon^{-1}=1+\sqrt[3]{2}+\sqrt[3]{4}$).

questions.q: Which fields below have unit rank exactly $2$?
choices: $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{3})$ — totally real of degree $4$, signature $(4,0)$, rank $3$.
$\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_7)$ — degree $6$, signature $(0,3)$.
$\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{5})$ — degree $3$, signature $(1,1)$, rank $1$.
A totally complex sextic field with signature $(0,3)$, e.g. $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_9)$.
questions.explain: Rank is $r_1+r_2-1$. Option 0: $4+0-1=3$. Option 1: $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_7)$ has $0+3-1=2$. ✓ Option 2: $1+1-1=1$. Option 3: $0+3-1=2$. ✓ The unit rank depends only on the number of archimedean places $r_1+r_2$, not on the degree alone — totally complex fields have half as many archimedean places as totally real fields of the same degree.

questions.q: Which classical theorem provides the geometric tool used to show $\ell(\mathcal{O}_K^\times)$ has full rank $r_1+r_2-1$ in the trace-zero hyperplane?
choices: Hensel's lemma.
Minkowski's convex-body theorem.
The Chinese remainder theorem.
Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions.
questions.explain: Minkowski's geometry of numbers — a centrally symmetric convex body of volume exceeding $2^n\,\mathrm{covol}(\Lambda)$ contains a nonzero lattice point — is applied to a stretched fundamental domain of $\mathcal{O}_K\subset K_\mathbb{R}=\mathbb{R}^{r_1}\times\mathbb{C}^{r_2}$ to manufacture units whose log-vectors span the hyperplane. The same Minkowski machine gives finiteness of the class group; Dirichlet's two big theorems (units and ideals) come from one geometric source.

questions.q: Compute $R_K$ for $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$. The fundamental unit is $\varepsilon=1+\sqrt{2}\approx 2.4142$. Give $R_K$ to three decimals.
questions.explain: Signature $(2,0)$, so the log-embedding lands in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the trace-zero hyperplane is the line $x_1+x_2=0$. The image of $\varepsilon=1+\sqrt{2}$ is $(\log(1+\sqrt{2}),\log|1-\sqrt{2}|)=(\log(1+\sqrt{2}),-\log(1+\sqrt{2}))$ since $(1+\sqrt{2})(1-\sqrt{2})=-1$. Drop one coordinate: the regulator is the absolute value of the remaining entry, $R_K=\log(1+\sqrt{2})\approx 0.8814$.

questions.q: Why is the regulator independent of the choice of fundamental units $\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_{r-1}$?
choices: Because all fundamental units are roots of unity.
Two choices of fundamental units differ by a $\mathrm{GL}_{r-1}(\mathbb{Z})$ matrix, whose determinant is $\pm 1$, so $|\det|$ of the log-coordinate matrix is invariant.
Because the regulator is always $1$.
By the Chebotarev density theorem.
questions.explain: Any two $\mathbb{Z}$-bases of the free part of $\mathcal{O}_K^\times$ are related by a $\mathrm{GL}_{r-1}(\mathbb{Z})$ change of basis (integer matrix with integer inverse, hence determinant $\pm 1$). The regulator is the determinant of an $(r-1)\times(r-1)$ minor of the log-coordinate matrix; multiplying by such a base-change matrix multiplies the determinant by $\pm 1$, leaving $|R_K|$ unchanged.

Signature $(0,1)$, so unit rank is $0+1-1=0$. The unit group is $\mathcal{O}_K^\times=\mu_K=\{\pm 1,\pm i\}$, all torsion. With no fundamental units to span anything, the regulator is the determinant of the empty matrix, conventionally $R_K=1$. The class number formula then reads $\mathrm{Res}_{s=1}\zeta_K(s)=2\pi h_K/(w_K\sqrt{|\Delta_K|})=2\pi/(4\cdot 2)=\pi/4$, recovering Dirichlet's class number formula for $\mathbb{Q}(i)$.

questions.q: In the analytic class number formula $\mathrm{Res}_{s=1}\zeta_K(s)=\frac{2^{r_1}(2\pi)^{r_2}\,h_K\,R_K}{w_K\sqrt{|\Delta_K|}}$, which two factors directly encode the failure of unique factorization at the level of elements?
choices: $h_K$ (the class number) and $R_K$ (the regulator).
$w_K$ and $\Delta_K$.
$\Delta_K$ and $w_K$.
questions.explain: $h_K$ measures how badly principal ideals miss being all ideals (failure of UFD), and $R_K$ measures the volume of the lattice of units (the multiplicative side, controlling how non-unique generators of principal ideals are). The $2^{r_1}(2\pi)^{r_2}$ is the archimedean local factor, $w_K$ is the torsion in the unit group, and $\sqrt{|\Delta_K|}$ is the global discriminant — these are normalizations, not the obstructions themselves.

questions.q: Where does the factor $\sqrt{|\Delta_K|}$ in the class number formula come from?
choices: It is the order of the Galois group.
It is the covolume of $\mathcal{O}_K$ as a lattice in $K\otimes_\mathbb{Q}\mathbb{R}\cong\mathbb{R}^{r_1}\times\mathbb{C}^{r_2}$.
It is the discriminant of the unit lattice.
It is the residue of $\zeta(s)$ at $s=1$.
questions.explain: Up to a normalization $2^{-r_2}$, $\sqrt{|\Delta_K|}$ is the covolume of $\mathcal{O}_K$ inside the Minkowski space $K_\mathbb{R}\cong\mathbb{R}^{r_1+2r_2}$. The class number formula is essentially a counting statement: the number of ideals of norm $\le X$ grows like $X\cdot$(residue), and the residue assembles the additive lattice covolume $\sqrt{|\Delta_K|}$, the multiplicative lattice covolume $R_K$, the torsion $w_K$, and the class group size $h_K$ into one coherent local-to-global product.

questions.q: For the rationals $K=\mathbb{Q}$ (signature $(1,0)$, $h=1$, $R=1$, $w=2$, $\Delta=1$), the class number formula reduces to $\mathrm{Res}_{s=1}\zeta(s)=2\cdot 1\cdot 1/(2\cdot 1)$. What numerical residue does this predict?
questions.explain: Plugging in: $\mathrm{Res}_{s=1}\zeta(s)=\frac{2^1(2\pi)^0\cdot 1\cdot 1}{2\cdot\sqrt{1}}=\frac{2}{2}=1$, matching the well-known fact that $\zeta(s)\sim 1/(s-1)$ near $s=1$. So the analytic class number formula contains the harmonic-series divergence as the simplest case — every step up in degree adds a regulator and a class number factor on top of this baseline.

du-pell-real-quadratic.title: Real quadratic units and Pell's equation

questions.q: The fundamental unit of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{3})$ is $\varepsilon=2+\sqrt{3}$. Verify Pell: compute $x^2-3y^2$ for $(x,y)=(2,1)$.
questions.explain: $2^2-3\cdot 1^2=4-3=1$, so $(2,1)$ is a solution of $x^2-3y^2=1$. The continued fraction of $\sqrt{3}=[1;\overline{1,2}]$ has period $2$, and the convergent at the end of the first period is $p_1/q_1=2/1$, giving exactly the fundamental solution. Powers $(2+\sqrt{3})^n$ then enumerate all positive Pell solutions: $(7,4),(26,15),(97,56),\ldots$.

questions.q: Why does the continued-fraction algorithm applied to $\sqrt{d}$ produce the fundamental unit of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$?
choices: Because all units of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ are rational.

By Lagrange's theorem the expansion is purely periodic past $a_0$, and the convergent at the end of one period is a solution of $x^2-dy^2=\pm 1$ — and a minimality argument among convergents shows it is the fundamental one.
Because every quadratic irrational is a Liouville number.
By Hensel's lemma.
questions.explain: Lagrange (1770): real quadratic irrationals have eventually-periodic continued fractions, and $\sqrt{d}$ for $d>0$ non-square is purely periodic after $a_0$. The Pell relation $p_{n-1}^2-d q_{n-1}^2=(-1)^n$ at the end of the period — easy to derive from the matrix product encoding of convergents — and a minimality argument show this convergent is the fundamental Pell solution, equivalently the smallest unit $>1$.

questions.q: For $d=2$, the fundamental unit is $1+\sqrt{2}$ with $N(1+\sqrt{2})=(1+\sqrt{2})(1-\sqrt{2})=-1$. So Pell's equation $x^2-2y^2=-1$ has solutions. For which $d$ is $x^2-dy^2=-1$ solvable?
choices: Only when $d$ is prime.
Always — for every squarefree $d>0$.
Iff the period of $\sqrt{d}$'s continued fraction is odd, equivalently iff $N(\varepsilon_d)=-1$ for the fundamental unit. (E.g. solvable for $d=2,5,10,13,\ldots$, unsolvable for $d=3,7,11,\ldots$.)
Iff $d\equiv 1\bmod 4$.
questions.explain: The negative Pell equation $x^2-dy^2=-1$ is solvable iff the fundamental unit has norm $-1$, equivalently iff the continued-fraction period of $\sqrt{d}$ is odd. For $d=3$ the period is $[1;\overline{1,2}]$ of length $2$ (even), so $N(\varepsilon_3)=N(2+\sqrt{3})=1$ and $x^2-3y^2=-1$ has no integer solutions. The density of $d$ for which the negative Pell is solvable is governed by Stevenhagen's conjecture, recently proven by Koymans–Pagano.

questions.q: Let $K=\mathbb{Q}$ and $S=\{\infty,2,3\}$. What is the rank of $\mathcal{O}_{K,S}^\times=\mathbb{Z}[1/6]^\times$?
questions.explain: The $S$-unit theorem gives rank $|S|-1=3-1=2$. Concretely $\mathbb{Z}[1/6]^\times=\{\pm 2^a 3^b:a,b\in\mathbb{Z}\}\cong\{\pm 1\}\times\mathbb{Z}^2$, with the two free generators $2$ and $3$ contributed by the two finite places in $S$.

questions.q: Which of the following are corollaries of the $S$-unit theorem and/or the $S$-unit equation theorem?
choices: For any number field $K$ and finite $S$, $\mathcal{O}_{K,S}^\times$ is finitely generated.
The equation $u+v=1$ has only finitely many solutions $(u,v)$ with $u,v\in\mathcal{O}_{K,S}^\times$ (Mahler / Evertse).
Every Diophantine equation has only finitely many integer solutions.
Siegel's theorem: an affine curve of geometric genus $\ge 1$ over a number field has only finitely many $S$-integral points.
questions.explain: The $S$-unit theorem itself gives finite generation (option 0). The $S$-unit equation theorem (Mahler 1933 in $\mathbb{Q}$, Evertse in general) gives option 1. Siegel's finiteness theorem for integral points on curves of genus $\ge 1$ reduces to the $S$-unit equation via the embedding into Jacobians (option 3). Option 2 is false: Pell and many others have infinitely many solutions.

questions.q: What replaces the archimedean log $\log|\sigma_v(\cdot)|$ in the log-embedding when extending to a finite (non-archimedean) place $v$ in $S$?
choices: The trivial map (finite places contribute nothing).
$-v(\cdot)\log Nv$, where $v$ is the normalised valuation and $Nv$ is the size of the residue field.
The $p$-adic logarithm $\log_p$.
The Frobenius automorphism.
questions.explain: Each finite place $v\in S$ contributes one extra coordinate $\log|x|_v=-v(x)\log Nv$ to the log-embedding. The product formula $\prod_v|x|_v=1$ (now over all places) again confines the image to a hyperplane of codimension $1$, and the same Minkowski-style argument shows the image is a lattice of full rank $|S|-1$ in this hyperplane — the kernel is still $\mu_K$.
